plot_extraction.response_text:
A once-celebrated actor, Kostromsky, returns to the provincial theatre where his career began to perform Hamlet. Though rumors abound that alcoholism and debauchery have ruined his talent, the performance sells out on the strength of his fame. Backstage, he drinks heavily while reassuring himself that his genius remains intact.

When the actress playing Ophelia suddenly falls ill, Yureva, a modest young student and devoted admirer of Kostromsky, agrees to replace her. Kostromsky begins the play brilliantly, but quickly exhausts his dwindling emotional powers. Meanwhile, Yureva gives an increasingly compelling performance, drawing the audience’s attention away from him. During Hamlet’s famous soliloquy, Kostromsky realizes with devastating clarity that the public is now indifferent to his acting and that his fame and talent are irretrievably fading.

Consumed by jealousy, he insults Yureva during the performance and later roughly pushes her aside after the audience enthusiastically recalls her. He then abandons the unfinished play, removes his makeup, and weeps alone as he confronts the ruin caused by arrogance, selfishness, and drink. Hearing Yureva crying backstage, he is overcome by remorse and compassion. He admits that he attacked her because her success forced him to recognize his own decline, acknowledges her genuine talent, and advises her to leave the stage as soon as she feels her artistic gift fading rather than wait for the public to reject her. He then walks away from the theatre, refusing even his payment and declaring his career finished.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story is written in a psychologically observant, realist mode, with the theatrical setting supplying an undercurrent of melodrama and tragedy. Its central stylistic device is dramatic irony: Kostromsky performs Hamlet while undergoing his own crisis of belated self-recognition. Shakespearean motifs—madness, mortality, displaced succession, wounded pride and thoughts of self-destruction—are woven into the actor’s collapse, so that the play within the story becomes both a mirror of his condition and the instrument that exposes it.

The narration is third-person omniscient but concentrates closely on Kostromsky’s consciousness. It moves readily from external description into authoritative psychological explanation, often stating motives and emotional conditions directly: his vanity, exhaustion, envy and fear are interpreted rather than merely implied. At important moments the perspective adopts his own rhythms and values through exclamations, rhetorical questions and fragments of inward speech. Yureva’s feelings are also briefly entered, but she remains comparatively idealised and serves chiefly as a foil to him: youth against decline, sincerity against mannerism, and instinctive talent against fame sustained by habit.

The diction is formal, literary and recognisably period-bound, with occasional archaic or translated constructions. Phrases such as “billet-doux,” “erstwhile beautiful face,” “illimitable pride,” and “empoisoned by the venom of grief” create an elevated register, while theatrical and social details give the prose concrete historical texture. Russian names, patronymics, roubles, provincial touring companies and hierarchical forms of address establish the milieu without prolonged exposition. Some idioms and syntactic inversions have the slightly stiff quality of an older English translation, and the spelling “Shakspeare” reinforces that period character.

Sentence structure alternates between long, cumulative passages and short emphatic statements. Extended sentences are used for biography, public reputation and psychological analysis, often accumulating clauses to convey the scale of Kostromsky’s former success or the pressure of his thoughts. Brief sentences—“There was no applause,” “It was a moment of awful enlightenment,” “Yes, it was all past!”—mark reversals and deliver emotional blows. Ellipses, dashes, repetitions and exclamation marks reproduce hesitation, intoxication and agitation, particularly in dialogue and interior monologue. The prose frequently intensifies through lists, as in the catalogue of wreaths, gifts, applause, money and female admiration that reduces Kostromsky’s glorious past to fading images.

Dialogue is strongly characterising and socially stratified. Kostromsky’s speech shifts between grandiose self-mythologising, imperious abuse, drunken vulgarity and, at the end, unexpectedly lucid tenderness. The barber’s stammering deference and the manager’s frantic colloquialism reveal the theatre’s hierarchy and backstage disorder. Yureva speaks little and softly, which enhances her modesty and leaves her acting to carry her emotional force. Yakovlef’s conversation introduces the experienced professional’s judgment and foreshadows Yureva’s triumph, making the later reversal feel inevitable rather than accidental.

The descriptive method relies on vivid visual and auditory contrasts. Backstage reality is rough, shabby and mechanical: cardboard scenery, hammering carpenters, greasepaint, gas burners and discarded stage properties. In front of the curtain, the theatre becomes a charged collective organism, murmuring like a distant sea, sighing “from a thousand breasts,” or erupting in applause. Recurrent imagery of crowds, chains, currents and enchantment represents the mysterious bond between performer and audience. Make-up and mirrors form another major motif. At first cosmetics appear to restore Kostromsky’s nobility and vitality; at the end, paint mingles with tears as the constructed public self dissolves. Light likewise gives way to darkness, moving from blazing footlights to the dim, dismantled stage after the failed performance.

The structure is linear and tightly theatrical, divided into eight numbered sections that function almost like scenes or acts. The opening establishes Kostromsky’s fame and hints at its decay; the emergency casting of Yureva initiates the conflict; successive acts of *Hamlet* chart the transfer of the audience’s attention; and the empty theatre provides the aftermath. Pacing slows at moments of recognition, especially when Kostromsky receives no applause and suddenly understands his decline. Repetition across the performance—entrances, applause, returns to the wings and demands for vodka—measures his deterioration with almost mechanical precision.

The tone combines irony, compassion and moral severity. Kostromsky is exposed as vain, selfish, cruel and alcoholic, yet the narration does not reduce him to a caricature. His final recognition grants him tragic dignity, though not absolution. Yureva’s talent is presented in lyrical and sentimental terms, while Kostromsky’s envy becomes nearly grotesque in its violent fantasies. The conclusion softens this harshness through confession and pity: he recognises both her gift and his injustice, then warns her against repeating his fate. His repeated declaration, “I have finished,” closes the story with the finality of a curtain falling.

Overall, the style blends backstage realism, explicit psychological narration and tragic theatrical symbolism. It is emotionally expansive rather than understated, using elevated language, foreshadowing and climactic reversals to portray artistic decline as a form of death. The dominant effect is that of a moral-psychological tragedy in miniature, in which public applause is both intoxicating and merciless, and the artist’s deepest catastrophe is not failure itself but the sudden recognition that the power which once justified his life has already departed.

# THE LAST HAMLET

## I

The news that Alexander Petrovitch Kostromsky was to appear in the provincial theatre travelled through the town with that singular rapidity which belongs only to reports of fires, murders, bankruptcies, and the coming of celebrated actors.

The walls were covered with yellow bills. Kostromsky’s name, printed in enormous black letters, towered above those of the local company as a church cupola towers above poor wooden cottages. At the pastry-cook’s, in the club, in the corridors of the district court, and even beneath the whispering arches of the cathedral porch, people spoke of him. Elderly ladies remembered having seen him twenty years before in Petersburg; young ladies, who knew him only from lithographs, repeated anecdotes of his passions and his magnificence; officers wagered as to whether he would be sober enough to finish the performance.

“He was a genius,” said some.

“He is still a genius,” objected others.

“He is a drunkard,” declared the more practical.

Yet nobody intended to remain at home.

Kostromsky had begun his career in that very theatre. Forty years earlier, a lean, dark-eyed youth with a hoarse voice and ungovernable pride, he had crossed its stage carrying a spear in a historical melodrama. There he had played his first lover, his first villain, his first madman; there, after a performance of Othello, the students had unharnessed the horses from his sledge and dragged him through the snow; there a governor’s wife had sent him a diamond ring in a billet-doux scented with violets. The town cherished these memories as though his celebrity reflected honour upon every inhabitant.

Afterwards came Moscow, Petersburg, Warsaw, Kiev, triumphs without number, wreaths with golden inscriptions, silver cups, velvet albums, money thrown away by handfuls, women, suppers, quarrels, journeys, champagne. For thirty years his name had drawn crowds. He had been compared with Garrick, Mochalov, Salvini; critics had found in his voice thunder, music, tears, prophecy. He himself had long ceased to doubt that nature had created the drama principally in order that he might interpret it.

But fame, which forgives almost everything while it is young, becomes exacting in old age. During recent seasons reports had grown malicious. It was said that Kostromsky forgot his words, that his hands trembled, that his once flexible voice had acquired a cracked metallic sound. In Kharkov he had fallen asleep in a dressing-room while the orchestra repeated an entr’acte three times; in Odessa he had struck a prompter; at Kazan he had appeared as King Lear with one boot unbuttoned and had addressed Cordelia by the name of Desdemona.

The reports reached him, but did not convince him. He knew very well that he drank; he knew that his memory had become treacherous and that, after the second act, an intolerable weariness sometimes filled his bones. But genius—was not genius immortal? Could wine drown what God had bestowed? Could a few provincial fools judge Alexander Kostromsky?

He arrived at noon in a hired troika, wearing a fur coat with a sable collar rubbed bare at the edges. The station-master, two reporters, the theatrical manager, and a deputation of admirers awaited him. Flowers were presented; speeches were made. Kostromsky bowed with his old majestic negligence. His broad-brimmed hat, grey locks, and aquiline profile produced an effect. Only at close quarters could one perceive that his cheeks were swollen, his eyelids inflamed, and the skin about his mouth traversed by innumerable fine wrinkles.

“We welcome in you our own glorious son!” cried the manager, Fedor Fedorovitch Babanov.

“My first cradle,” replied Kostromsky, looking past him at the station buffet. “Yes, my dear fellow, my artistic cradle.”

He drank three glasses of brandy before entering the carriage.

By evening no seat remained unsold for either of the two performances announced. Hamlet was to be given first, and on the following night The Robbers. The manager rubbed his hands, rushed through the theatre shouting at carpenters and dressers, and calculated receipts with an agitation resembling religious ecstasy.

Kostromsky slept until five. When he awoke, the winter twilight already pressed blue and heavy against the hotel windows. For several minutes he did not know where he was. His head ached; his tongue seemed coated with ashes; one hand, lying upon the coverlet, trembled.

Then he saw the bouquet on the table and remembered.

Hamlet!

He rang and ordered tea, cognac, lemons, hot water, raw eggs, and a bottle of champagne. Looking into the spotted mirror above the washstand, he was startled by his own face. It appeared old—not artistically old, not the noble pallor of a soul exhausted by thought, but coarsely, pitilessly old. He thrust back his grey hair.

“Nonsense!” he murmured. “A face is clay. Give me twenty minutes before the mirror.”

Yet uneasiness had entered him. It remained even after the cognac had warmed his stomach and restored to his gestures something of their former breadth.

He remembered the theatre—the low ceiling, the narrow stage, the damp smell in the passages—and smiled. To return as Hamlet to the boards where he had once carried a spear! There was poetry in that. There was destiny. The public would see that the old lion still possessed his claws.

“The rest are tradesmen,” he said aloud. “They perform. I create.”

And, pleased by the phrase, he repeated it as he dressed.

## II

Behind the curtain, two hours before the performance, the theatre displayed none of that enchanted magnificence which the audience afterwards ascribes to it. Bare brick walls rose above crooked flats; ropes hung like gallows cords; a painted tomb leaned against a woodland brook; Denmark’s battlements were supported from behind by cracked planks and flour barrels. Carpenters hammered, property-men quarrelled, chorus girls ran through the passages half dressed, and somewhere a child cried because a dresser had pinched her finger.

The gas burners hissed. The odour of dust, damp cloth, glue, greasepaint, perspiration and cheap scent made the air heavy.

Kostromsky sat before his mirror in dressing-room number one. An old barber named Semyon, who claimed to have shaved him at his first benefit performance, was whitening his temples and fastening a dark wig over the actor’s grey hair.

“More shadow beneath the eyes,” Kostromsky commanded.

“Yes, Alexander Petrovitch.”

“And straighten the left eyebrow. You have made me look like a frightened deacon.”

“I beg pardon, Alexander Petrovitch. My hands—seeing you again after so many years—my hands won’t obey me.”

“Then borrow another pair.”

The old man stammered an apology. Kostromsky smiled at the mirror. The paint was performing its merciful deception. Under its warm brown tones the swollen flesh withdrew, wrinkles vanished, the nose acquired greater nobility, and the eyes, outlined in black, seemed larger and more melancholy. The Prince of Denmark looked back at him.

There! What had he feared? The face alone could command an audience.

On the table stood a glass and a bottle of vodka. From time to time he drank, afterwards biting a slice of apple. The alcohol did not intoxicate him; so at least he believed. It merely drew a curtain between him and fatigue, calmed the mutiny of his nerves, and awakened in his breast that generous heat which he mistook for inspiration.

The door opened without ceremony, and Babanov thrust in his bald head.

“A misfortune, Alexander Petrovitch! A catastrophe! I am a ruined man!”

“What is it?”

“Maria Andreyevna. Fever—chills—she cannot stand. She is lying on the sofa like a corpse. Ophelia! We have no Ophelia!”

Kostromsky continued to inspect his eyebrows.

“Give the part to someone else.”

“To whom? Surovtseva does not know it. The soubrette says Shakspeare gives her neuralgia. We shall have to return the money. Fourteen hundred roubles, not counting the boxes! My God, why was I born?”

In the passage voices rose. Someone wept; someone ran for the doctor. Kostromsky poured himself another vodka.

“Is there not a single young woman in this educational metropolis capable of learning Ophelia?”

“There is Yureva,” said Babanov suddenly. “But she—no, impossible.”

“Who is Yureva?”

“A pupil. A student of the dramatic class. She has never played before the public. She knows the role, I think. She attends every rehearsal when she is permitted.”

“Then let her play.”

Babanov stared.

“Beside you?”

“Why not? A block of wood can play Ophelia if Hamlet plays Hamlet.”

At that moment another actor entered. This was Pavel Nikolaitch Yakovlef, an elderly member of the company who had known poverty, success, provincial winters, managerial swindles, and every humiliation of his profession. His Claudius was considered sound, though Kostromsky had privately described it as the work of a conscientious undertaker.

“Yureva can do it,” Yakovlef said. “I have heard her at the school.”

“A schoolgirl?” asked Kostromsky.

“She has instinct.”

“Instinct! Every cat has instinct.”

“Not every actress.”

Kostromsky shrugged.

“Bring her. But tell her not to scream. Young women imagine madness is a toothache.”

Ten minutes later Yureva stood at the dressing-room door. She was dressed in a plain brown gown, for she had been summoned from the gallery where she had come to see her idol. She was scarcely twenty. Her figure was slight; her fair hair was arranged without elegance, and her face, pale from alarm, possessed no regular beauty. Only her eyes were remarkable—grey, candid, and attentive, with that luminous seriousness sometimes seen in children who have known sorrow too early.

She looked at Kostromsky, and her lips parted. For years she had kept his portrait above her writing-table. His Hamlet, known to her through descriptions, had become for her one of those impossible summits toward which youth gazes without considering roads, hunger, storms, or death.

“Do you know the part?” he asked.

“Yes, Alexander Petrovitch.”

“All of it?”

“Yes.”

“Have you played it?”

“Only at the class.”

“Before how many?”

“Twelve.”

He laughed.

“To-night there are nine hundred. But never mind; they are only twelve people multiplied by seventy-five. Do as I direct, keep your eyes on me, and do not seek effects. Above all, do not interfere.”

“I shall try not to disgrace you,” she said softly.

The humility of the words pleased him.

“You will not disgrace me, child. No one can do that but I myself—and I have not yet acquired the habit.”

Yakovlef glanced at him, but remained silent.

Yureva was led away to be dressed. In the corridor Babanov wrung her hand and talked so rapidly that she understood nothing. Costumes were fetched, rejected, pinned and altered. The sick actress’s shoes proved too small; her white gown was too wide at the shoulders. Dressers pulled at Yureva as though she were a doll to be repaired before presentation.

Only when she heard the orchestra tuning beyond the curtain did terror seize her. Nine hundred persons! The thought had no human proportions. It was a black sea waiting behind a wall. She pressed her hands together and whispered the first lines of Ophelia.

Yakovlef passed and paused beside her.

“Do not think of them,” he said.

“How can I avoid it?”

“Think of the man to whom you speak. If he is Hamlet to you, they will believe you are Ophelia.”

“And if I fail?”

“Then you will have learned what cannot be taught in twelve lessons.”

He looked at her closely.

“Do not imitate Kostromsky.”

She flushed, as though he had uttered blasphemy.

“Why should I not?”

“Because one Kostromsky is enough. And perhaps”—the old actor lowered his voice—“more than enough.”

## III

The bell rang.

That sound, which to a spectator is merely a warning to settle into his chair, passes through an actor’s nerves like an electrical current. The confusion behind the scenes sharpened and became purposeful. The players took their places; the prompter descended into his wooden shell; Babanov peeped through a hole in the curtain and came away radiant.

“Not an empty chair! The governor! The marshal of nobility! Every student in town!”

Kostromsky stood in the wings, his black cloak falling in severe folds. He could hear the audience: a vast, subdued murmur, resembling the sound of the sea within a shell. From this breathing darkness fame had come to him; from it had come money, love, insolence, life itself. He knew the creature. He had mastered it a thousand times.

The curtain rose upon Elsinore.

While the sentinels spoke, he waited calmly. His pulse was even. He had taken enough vodka to steady himself, not enough to cloud his articulation. A pleasant emptiness filled his head, leaving room for the part.

His entrance was greeted first by silence and then by applause which spread from the stalls to the gallery, gathering force until the scene itself seemed to tremble. Kostromsky did not bow. Hamlet, he held, must not acknowledge clapping. But he delayed one instant, standing in profile beneath the blue stage light, and allowed the audience to contemplate him.

The applause increased.

Ah! What fools had dared speak of decline?

He began.

His first words were uttered almost carelessly, with a dry, inward bitterness which startled those who expected declamation. The voice, though no longer full, carried to the remotest corner. In the court scene he scarcely moved; a slight contraction of the mouth, a lifted eyelid, the cold inclination of his head toward the King—these sufficed. The spectators bent forward. When he remained alone and grief at last broke through the ceremonial restraint, his sorrow seemed enormous because it had been so long confined.

The old enchantment was accomplished.

Backstage, even the carpenters ceased hammering. Babanov wiped his brow and whispered, “A miracle.” Yakovlef, waiting for his entrance, watched without expression. Yureva stood behind a flat, pale and motionless.

Kostromsky felt the public yield. Its attention ran toward him in invisible currents; nine hundred separate souls were fastened to his gesture. He could pause as long as he pleased, and no one coughed. He could lower his voice almost to a breath, and the silence leaned toward him to catch it.

When he came off, applause burst forth.

He walked to his dressing-room slowly, followed by congratulations.

“Well?” he said to the barber.

“Divine, Alexander Petrovitch! As in former days—no, greater!”

“As in former days?” Kostromsky repeated.

“I meant—your greatness cannot be measured by days.”

“Idiot. Pour me some vodka.”

He drank, sat down and closed his eyes. The act had cost him more than he expected. His shirt clung damply between his shoulders; his heart beat with small painful knocks. Formerly, after such a scene, he had felt expanded, refreshed, hungry for the next act. Now something within him had been spent at once, like powder in a flash.

But this was natural. He had travelled; he had slept badly. Besides, the first act was the heaviest.

In the corridor people were calling for Yureva. Her first scene approached. Kostromsky opened his eyes and saw her pass in the white gown, a wreath upon her fair hair.

“Come here.”

She obeyed.

“Do not tremble,” he said. “And remember: Ophelia loves Hamlet, but she also fears him. Love pulls you forward, fear holds you back. That is the whole mechanism.”

“Yes, Alexander Petrovitch.”

“Do not look at the audience.”

“No.”

“And do not weep too soon. Tears are the refuge of actresses who have nothing to say.”

She thanked him. Her grateful gaze again pleased his vanity, and for a moment he felt almost paternal.

The scene began.

At first Yureva’s voice was too low. Two or three people coughed. Kostromsky, entering, perceived her terror and instantly made use of it. His Hamlet approached with such concentrated anguish that she forgot the footlights. She saw not the celebrated actor who had spoken kindly to her in a dressing-room, but a beloved man whom some invisible catastrophe had torn away from her.

Her fear became Ophelia’s fear.

“Tell me,” he said, looking into her eyes.

She answered.

Something in the simplicity of her reply surprised him. There was no theatrical sweetness, no carefully modulated pathos. She spoke as a young girl would speak when truth is demanded by one whom she cannot deceive. At the next phrase her hand moved toward him and stopped midway, arrested by shame and dread. The gesture was unconscious. A sigh passed through the auditorium.

Kostromsky heard it.

For an instant he was irritated. Then professional instinct conquered. Her sincerity supported him; against its clear light his Hamlet grew darker and more terrible. He seized her wrist, rejected her, returned, searched her face as though begging for salvation while his words destroyed all hope. She responded to each change, not with studied attitudes but with the helpless accuracy of true feeling.

At the close of the scene there was applause. It began hesitantly, then became warm and prolonged.

Yureva fled into the wings, blinded by tears.

“They like you,” Babanov cried, embracing her shoulders.

She looked only for Kostromsky.

He came off more slowly. His breathing was laboured. She hurried toward him.

“Alexander Petrovitch—”

“Not badly,” he said. “For a beginning.”

Those around them murmured approval. Yakovlef smiled.

“Instinct,” he observed.

Kostromsky turned on him.

“She follows. That is all. A child can follow when she has someone to lead her.”

“Certainly,” Yakovlef answered.

The agreement sounded to Kostromsky more offensive than contradiction.

## IV

During the interval the audience discussed Yureva.

At first her name was not known. Programmes were examined, neighbours questioned, ushers summoned. The story of the sudden substitution passed from box to box. That a pupil should have faced the public without rehearsal and played with such truth seemed marvellous. Young men in the gallery declared her a discovery; ladies praised the purity of her face; an old colonel said she reminded him of an actress whom he had loved in 1862.

Kostromsky knew nothing of these conversations, yet by the obscure instinct developed in those who live upon applause he felt that attention had divided.

In his dressing-room he paced between table and door. The fatigue had deepened. His muscles seemed filled with cold sand. He poured vodka, found the bottle empty, and rang violently.

“Semyon!”

The barber appeared.

“Another bottle.”

“Alexander Petrovitch, perhaps tea—”

“Did I ask what you drink? Bring vodka.”

When alone, he looked into the mirror. The paint had cracked beside his nostrils. Perspiration shone upon his forehead. He repaired the damage with trembling fingers.

It was absurd to be disturbed by a schoolgirl. Her success belonged to him. Had he not steadied her? Had not his force drawn the feeling from her as a magnet draws iron? Beside a mediocre Hamlet she would be colourless. The audience applauded the scene, and the scene was his.

Nevertheless, he remembered the sigh that had passed through the theatre when she stretched out her hand.

Why had they sighed there? He had been speaking. He had created the anguish. Yet the sigh had gone to her.

Kostromsky drank as soon as the bottle arrived.

The next act began badly for him. The alcohol warmed his limbs but loosened the rein upon his art. His gestures became broader. He struck phrases which should have been allowed to fall softly; he rolled his eyes in a manner once admired by provincial critics; he prolonged pauses until they ceased to be pregnant and became merely empty.

He did not know this. The actor who is declining commonly becomes his own most indulgent spectator. He hears in a worn voice its former resonance, sees in an habitual gesture the passion that first produced it, and mistakes the obedience of technique for the fire of creation. Memory applauds while the public grows cold.

Kostromsky felt only that the audience resisted him. He therefore increased his efforts. He shouted where he had once whispered, rushed across the stage where he had once stood still, and threw himself into attitudes whose beauty belonged to a younger body.

The audience remained respectful. Respect is the first mourning garment of dead enthusiasm.

There was applause at the recognised points, but it came like payment of a debt. No spontaneous cry broke from the gallery. No electric shudder ran through the house. The mysterious chain had loosened.

Then Yureva entered.

Her first terror had vanished, but not her humility. She had discovered the audience and forgotten it almost in the same instant. Its attention no longer oppressed her; it sustained her as deep water sustains one who ceases to struggle. She thought only of Ophelia’s bewilderment, of the beloved mind into which she could no longer enter, of obedience to a father she feared and loyalty to a man she loved.

Kostromsky saw at once that she had grown.

This offended him as though the growth had taken something from his own stature.

In their encounter he altered a piece of business without warning, advancing upon her suddenly and speaking close to her face. It was a test, almost a trap. A trained but unimaginative actress would have lost the thread. Yureva recoiled; then, reading cruelty and pain in his expression, she gave a low cry so natural that the public stirred.

Again that murmur!

His fingers tightened about her arm.

“Go!” he said with real hatred beneath Hamlet’s madness.

She turned white. The terror in her eyes delighted and enraged him. For one hideous second he wished to crush her arm, to make her cry not as Ophelia but as herself, to punish the young blood in her cheeks, the clear voice, the future opening before her.

And because the hatred was real, the scene flamed. The audience believed it inspired.

When Yureva went off, applause followed her like a pursuing storm. She returned for a bow at Babanov’s frantic urging, though the act was not yet ended. The audience called her twice.

Kostromsky stood behind a flat and listened.

“Yureva! Yureva!”

Yesterday the town had not known her name.

He felt the cry pass through him like a knife.

Yakovlef approached, adjusting Claudius’s crown.

“Take care,” he said quietly.

“Of what?”

“You are tiring yourself.”

“Attend to your king and leave Hamlet to me.”

“I am speaking of the girl.”

“What girl?”

“You frightened her.”

“She is playing Ophelia. Ophelia must be frightened.”

“Not of the actor.”

Kostromsky laughed, but his lips were colourless beneath the paint.

“My dear Pavel Nikolaitch, when an old crow has acquired a few grey feathers, he begins to imagine himself an eagle. Do not teach me my art.”

“No,” said Yakovlef. “One could not teach you anything.”

Again the calm agreement struck harder than insolence.

## V

The famous soliloquy came in the fourth act of the provincial arrangement, after an interval during which Kostromsky drank twice and sat for several minutes with his head between his hands.

Once, “To be, or not to be” had been the crown of his Hamlet. Audiences awaited it with almost physical expectation. His interpretation was known throughout Russia. He began not as a philosopher entertaining an abstract question, but as a man to whom death had entered the room and taken a chair opposite him. The thought developed gradually; fear contended with longing; and at the end, when consciousness had made cowards of all, he appeared to awake from the very edge of the grave. Men who despised the theatre had wept.

He remembered every triumph attached to those lines: flowers falling from a box in Moscow, students shouting in Kiev, a woman fainting in Vilna, the critic who wrote that Kostromsky had “lifted the skull of mankind and looked beneath it.”

Now, as he waited in the darkness, he repeated to himself: This will restore everything.

The stage had been cleared. A cold light lay upon the painted corridor. Beyond the footlights the auditorium was invisible, yet he could feel its thousand eyes. It had applauded Yureva; very well. In a moment it would remember whom it had come to see.

He entered.

The silence was complete.

“To be, or not to be—”

His voice sounded strange to him, too near and too dry. He paused.

Formerly the first sentence had opened within him an abyss. Now he saw only a sentence, famous, dangerous, worn smooth by repetition. He knew how to incline his head, when to raise his hand, where to let the voice sink, where to summon its bronze vibration. All was prepared, arranged, classified. But behind the mechanism there was nothing.

He continued.

He spoke of death while fearing not death but indifference. He spoke of the undiscovered country while thinking of the gallery. He spoke of the whips and scorns of time, and suddenly the words, long dulled by use, recovered an atrocious personal meaning.

The whips and scorns of time!

Was not time standing before him now, pitiless, invisible, holding up the young girl as evidence? Yureva had not defeated him. Time had chosen her as its instrument. Youth had entered in a borrowed white gown and, with one unconscious gesture, overturned the throne built from thirty years of applause.

He reached the line where Hamlet meditates upon the proud man’s contumely. His breath failed. A cough sounded in the stalls.

A cough!

In former days no one had breathed.

He made the great pause—the pause which had been described in journals and imitated by dozens of actors. The audience waited politely. From somewhere in the upper gallery came the rustle of a programme.

He finished.

There was no applause.

Perhaps a few hands moved uncertainly, but the sound died before it became clapping. The silence which followed was not the silence of enchantment. It was vacancy. The audience had listened because the words were Shakspeare’s and the actor was Kostromsky; it had waited for the celebrated effect; the effect had not come.

It was a moment of awful enlightenment.

Kostromsky stood upon the stage, but another self, sober, merciless, and all-seeing, stood apart and judged him. The paint, the black cloak, the noble attitude—what were they? Rags hung upon an exhausted old man. The voice? A broken instrument. The gestures? Echoes. The grief? Memory of grief. He had spent his gift years ago, squandered it in drinking rooms, at card tables, in embraces without love, in quarrels undertaken to nourish vanity. For a long time fame had concealed the loss. Managers had advertised the name; audiences had applauded the legend; critics had respectfully compared the ruin with the palace once standing there. And he, fool, drunkard, sovereign of an empty kingdom, had believed himself immortal.

Yes, it was all past!

Wreaths, diamonds, horses unharnessed, women at hotel doors, suppers until dawn, banknotes thrust into waiters’ hands, the roar of crowded houses, young actors trembling in his presence—where were they? Painted scraps, like the cardboard battlements of Elsinore, splendid from the auditorium and propped behind by dirty planks.

He had thought himself Hamlet. He was only the ghost.

The thought struck him with such force that he swayed. The prompter whispered the next line. Kostromsky looked toward the little hooded box with hatred.

“I know!” he cried.

The words were not in the play.

The audience stirred. He recovered himself and continued, but now consciousness pursued him. Every intonation appeared false before it left his mouth. He anticipated each gesture and despised it while making it. His own body had become an enemy which parodied the actor he once had been.

When he came offstage, no one congratulated him.

Babanov busied himself with a property sword. Semyon pretended to arrange the cloak. A young scene-shifter, not knowing whom to fear, stared openly.

“Vodka,” Kostromsky said.

No one moved.

“Are you deaf?”

The barber hurried away.

From the stage came Yureva’s voice.

It was the mad scene.

## VI

Yureva had sat alone before her entrance, wounded and bewildered by Kostromsky’s cruelty. She could still feel the pressure of his fingers upon her arm. She believed she had offended him through inexperience. Perhaps she had stood in the wrong place; perhaps her applause had delayed the performance; perhaps—and this thought was most painful—her acting had been vulgar, and the audience’s approval had merely irritated a great artist who perceived its falsity.

She wept quietly.

Then the call-boy summoned her.

Ophelia enters mad after a grief too great for her frail understanding. Yureva had rehearsed the scene many times, adorning it with broken laughter, wandering looks, and picturesque gestures copied from celebrated actresses. Now all those devices seemed shameful. Her own heart was bruised; admiration, fear, humiliation and pity had confused it. She stepped before the footlights carrying this confusion with her.

At first the spectators scarcely recognised her. Her fair hair hung loose; bits of straw and withered flowers clung to her white gown. She smiled.

The smile was not madness exhibited, but sanity trying with pathetic courtesy to conceal its wound.

The theatre became still.

She sang. Her voice, small and without extraordinary beauty, trembled once, steadied itself, and floated through the house with an innocence more piercing than any lamentation. She distributed flowers which were not there, naming them as though each invisible blossom preserved a memory. At moments she seemed to listen for someone who would never answer. Then she laughed, and in that laugh there was the clear note of something broken forever.

Behind the scenery Kostromsky listened.

Every phrase reached the place in him newly laid bare by humiliation. He knew acting; whatever jealousy might say, he could not be deceived in this. The girl possessed the gift. Not discipline, not experience, not knowledge—these might come or might not—but the sacred and terrible capacity to feel before strangers without shame and to make their hearts beat in obedience to hers. She had crossed the footlights. She held the chain.

And he had lost it.

His first emotion was envy so violent that his sight darkened. He wanted her to fail, to forget a line, to trip over the gown, to force the audience to laugh. When the first sob came from the stalls, he clenched his hands.

“What nonsense,” he muttered. “Sentimental rubbish.”

No one answered.

Yureva approached the end of the scene. Her face turned toward the wings, and for one instant her eyes met Kostromsky’s. She saw him watching. The remembered insult entered her expression: love shrinking before cruelty, the disciple before the fallen idol, Ophelia before Hamlet. Without intending it, he completed her art.

She spoke her last words and went out as though drifting after something invisible.

For a second there was silence.

Then the theatre erupted.

Applause broke from nine hundred breasts at once, violent, joyous, almost savage. People rose. The gallery stamped. Handkerchiefs waved from the boxes. Voices called:

“Yureva! Yureva!”

She stopped in the wings, terrified by the noise.

“Go!” cried Babanov, pushing her forward. “Bow!”

She went before the curtain, bowed awkwardly, and returned.

The applause did not cease.

“Again!”

She went again. Someone threw roses. One struck her shoulder and fell at her feet.

Kostromsky watched from the passage. The sound was familiar—too familiar. It was the very storm that had once beaten around him. He recognised its degrees, its rising waves, the separate cry which provokes a renewed outbreak, the stamping by which the gallery expresses love when hands are insufficient. The public had not changed. It could still adore. It was he whom it no longer adored.

Yureva returned for the third time, flushed, trembling, with tears upon her cheeks. As she passed, her sleeve touched him.

He seized her shoulder.

“That is enough!”

She started.

“The public is calling,” Babanov protested.

“The public is a fool.”

Again the cries arose.

“Yureva!”

Babanov attempted to lead her back. Kostromsky pushed her aside with such violence that she struck the wall.

“You little fool!” he hissed. “Do you think those cattle love you? You grimace, whine, scatter your hair, and they call it art! Go—take your triumph! Feed upon it while it lasts!”

Her face became white. She looked at him with an expression in which pain gradually extinguished reverence.

That look was unbearable.

“Do not stare at me!”

“I am sorry,” she whispered.

“Sorry? For whom?”

“For you, Alexander Petrovitch.”

He raised his hand as though to strike her. Yakovlef stepped between them.

“Enough.”

The two men looked at each other.

Kostromsky’s hand fell.

From before the curtain came continued applause, then murmurs of surprise. The orchestra leader, uncertain what to do, lifted his baton and began the entr’acte. The musicians played too loudly.

“I shall not continue,” Kostromsky said.

Babanov laughed nervously.

“What do you mean?”

“I have finished.”

“But there is another act! The graveyard—the duel—the death! Alexander Petrovitch, my dear benefactor, they will smash the seats!”

“Let them.”

“You cannot abandon Hamlet before he dies!”

“He is dead.”

Kostromsky turned toward his dressing-room.

Babanov followed, wringing his hands.

“Think of the public! Think of my position! Think of the governor! We can shorten the act. Ten minutes—five! You may omit the fencing. Only die, Alexander Petrovitch! For the love of God, come out and die!”

The actor shut the door in his face.

## VII

For several minutes Kostromsky stood without moving.

Outside, Babanov pleaded, threatened, groaned, and finally ran away in search of Yakovlef. The orchestra continued to play. Its cheerful strains, intended to soothe the public, penetrated the thin door with an air of monstrous frivolity.

Kostromsky approached the mirror.

Hamlet confronted him.

The face was magnificent at a distance. White forehead, dark eyes, finely marked brows, a mouth compressed by thought—there was the portrait reproduced in albums and shop windows. But when he leaned nearer he saw the sweat eating channels through the paint, the sagging flesh under the chin, the inflamed veins beside the nose. The prince was melting. The old drunkard emerged.

He tore off the wig.

Grey hair, flattened and damp, fell about his skull. He rubbed his cheek with a towel. Flesh-coloured paint, black pencil and rouge smeared together. He rubbed harder, almost fiercely, as if the false face were a stain of which he must purify himself. The towel became filthy; the skin beneath burned red.

The mirror now showed neither Hamlet nor Kostromsky the genius, but Alexander Petrovitch, sixty-two years old, exhausted, frightened, alone.

He sat down.

On the wall hung his visiting costume, upon the table lay the skull used in the graveyard scene, its plaster forehead chipped above one eye. He picked it up.

“How many times?” he murmured.

How many times had he held that skull and spoken of Yorick? A thousand? Two thousand? He had made audiences meditate upon mortality while living as though no reckoning awaited him. He had preached the vanity of ambition in cities where he demanded larger letters on the posters. He had lamented the frailty of flesh and afterwards drunk until morning. Shakspeare had placed truth upon his tongue; he had converted it into effects.

The plaster skull grinned.

Kostromsky hurled it across the room. It struck the wall and broke.

Then he wept.

At first the tears came slowly, surprising him. He brushed them away with annoyance. But grief, once permitted entrance, rushed upon him with illimitable force. He bent over the table, his shoulders shaking. Paint mingled with tears and stained his hands.

He wept for his lost art, but also for his youth, and it was impossible to separate the two. He saw himself as he had been in that theatre: hungry, thin, arrogant, rehearsing beneath a single gas jet after midnight; believing that suffering ennobled him and every sacrifice was light because the future blazed ahead. What would that young man say if shown this ending? He would turn away in disgust. Or perhaps he would not believe it. Youth never believes in the old age it prepares for itself.

Kostromsky remembered chances rejected, friends insulted, women abandoned, parts neglected because supper had seemed more urgent than rehearsal. He remembered directors who warned him, physicians who begged him to stop drinking, an old actress who had said, “Guard your gift; it is not your property.” He had laughed at them all. The gift was inexhaustible! Applause would always arise! If one company dismissed him, ten managers would kneel at his hotel door!

Arrogance, selfishness, drink—three patient executioners. They had not killed him at once. They had taken a tone from his voice, a thought from his memory, a degree of truth from each gesture. Because the theft was gradual he had not perceived it. When at last he looked, the treasury was empty.

What remained to him? Touring small towns upon the credit of his name, deceiving audiences too timid to hiss? Playing kings who could not remember their kingdoms? Becoming an anecdote told in greenrooms: “I saw Kostromsky when he was great”? Waiting until managers ceased to answer his telegrams?

On the table lay a small razor used for trimming the wig. His gaze rested upon it.

To be, or not to be.

The irony was so cruel that he laughed through his tears. A real blade, a real question—and no audience! What admirable staging! He imagined the door forced open, Babanov shrieking, the newspapers: TRAGIC DEATH OF THE GREAT KOSTROMSKY. Flowers would come again. Obituaries would restore everything. Critics would forget the failed soliloquy and write of his immortal genius. Death might accomplish the effect denied to art.

He took up the razor.

The handle was light. The blade, poorly sharpened, reflected the gas flame.

But the impulse passed almost at once. Not courage restrained him, nor hope. He felt only weariness. Even death appeared another performance, and he had no strength left to play it.

He put down the razor.

The orchestra stopped. Beyond the door came confused noises: footsteps, angry voices, seats closing, the dull roar of a disappointed public. Babanov had evidently announced that the performance could not continue owing to sudden illness. Some spectators demanded their money; others lingered, hoping Yureva might appear once more.

The theatre gradually emptied.

Kostromsky sat in darkness after the gas burner began to fail. No one disturbed him. Babanov, having exhausted entreaties, had turned to financial disaster; the actors changed their clothes in silence. Stagehands commenced dismantling Elsinore before Hamlet’s death had taken place.

Presently, through the wall, Kostromsky heard someone crying.

The sound was soft and restrained. It came from the adjoining dressing-room.

Yureva.

He raised his head.

At first her tears irritated him. Why should she cry? She had triumphed. The future stood before her with flowers in its hands. To-night she had received in one hour what others begged for through years of humiliation.

Then he remembered the look in her eyes after he pushed her. He remembered her words: I am sorry for you.

He had struck at the only person in the theatre who had approached him with love. She had worshipped him; for that very reason he had desired to wound her. Her success had been innocent, yet he had treated it as treachery. What had she understood of his terror? She was a child suddenly dragged from the gallery, thrust into a white gown, and ordered to act beside a famous man. If she possessed talent, was that a crime?

The jealousy ebbed, leaving shame.

Compassion, long stifled by vanity but not wholly dead, stirred within him. Perhaps this was the final spark of the gift he had squandered: the power to enter, however late, into another’s suffering.

He rose and went to the door.

## VIII

The corridors were nearly dark. A solitary lamp burned beside the staircase; shadows of ropes and hanging costumes wavered upon the walls. Through the open door to the stage one could see workmen carrying away the painted walls of the palace. The footlights had been extinguished. Beyond them, the empty auditorium yawned like a cavern, its rows of red seats covered in grey gloom.

Yureva sat upon a trunk outside her dressing-room. She had changed into her brown gown, but her hair still hung loosely over her shoulders. The wreath lay crushed beside her. She covered her face with both hands.

Kostromsky stopped before her.

She heard him and rose quickly. Fear passed across her face.

“Do not be afraid,” he said.

His voice no longer possessed Hamlet’s resonance. It was the tired voice of an old man.

“I came to ask you to forgive me.”

She looked at him, uncertain whether this too might conceal cruelty.

“I behaved vilely,” he continued. “No—do not deny it out of politeness. I know the names of things now. For once I know them.”

“You were ill, Alexander Petrovitch.”

“I was envious.”

She lowered her eyes.

“Yes, envious of you. It sounds ridiculous, does it not? Kostromsky, whose name covers the walls, envious of a pupil without a pair of theatrical shoes. But the ridiculous is sometimes more painful than the sublime.”

He sat upon the trunk and passed a hand over his face. Without wig or paint, in the poor corridor light, he appeared suddenly ancient.

“You must understand,” he said. “When you played, the public listened to you as it once listened to me. I felt the current leave me and go toward you. An actor knows it. He may pretend, he may accuse the public, the author, the company, the weather—but he knows. To-night I knew.”

Yureva remained silent.

“I wanted to hurt you because you had shown me the truth. Not intentionally. You did not even look at me. That made it worse. If you had plotted to defeat me, I might have hated you honestly. But you merely felt. You opened your heart, and they followed you.”

“I could not have played without you,” she said. “When you looked at me—”

“Ah, yes. I looked at you with hatred. It was useful to Ophelia.”

“No. Before that. You made everything real.”

For a moment his old vanity raised its head. He felt the sweetness of her tribute and nearly accepted it as proof that his judgment had been mistaken. But enlightenment, once suffered, could not be entirely dismissed.

“I helped you,” he said. “Perhaps. A dying fire may light another candle. But do not confuse that with what I was. Nor with what I am.”

He looked toward the dismantled stage. A carpenter dropped a plank; the crash reverberated through the empty house.

“You have talent,” he said.

Yureva drew a breath.

“Yakovlef told me you had instinct. I laughed at him. He was right. You have more than instinct. You have sincerity, and sincerity upon the stage is rarer than beauty, intelligence, or voice. Guard it. Technique will come. Fame may come. Money, flowers, flatterers, fools with articles, women who envy you, men who swear they understand you—all may come. They will tell you that you are sacred because they desire to possess a little of your triumph. Do not believe them.”

She sat down at the opposite end of the trunk.

“Is fame so evil?”

“No. It is delightful. Poison is often delightful, otherwise no one would take it. Applause enters the blood more swiftly than vodka. One begins by needing it after a great performance; afterwards one needs it for entering, for speaking, for merely showing one’s face. At last one cannot live without the sound, though one has ceased to deserve it.”

He smiled bitterly.

“I was not always what you saw to-night. Remember that, if you can. I worked. I suffered. There were evenings when I gave them all I possessed and more—when something passed through me that did not belong to me, and I was afraid of it even while I rejoiced. That is why the ruin is so complete. If I had always been a charlatan, there would be nothing to mourn.”

“I know you were great,” Yureva whispered.

“Were. A small word! An abyss contained in four letters.”

She began to weep again, but now her tears were for him.

Kostromsky looked at her with tenderness. There was no desire in it, no vanity, no theatrical paternalism; only the grave compassion of one condemned traveller for another who has just set out upon the road.

“Listen to me, Anna Sergeyevna.”

She was startled that he knew her Christian name and patronymic.

“If your gift grows, serve it, not yourself. Do not imagine it is immortal because it burns brightly. Everything living can die. Work while it lives. Keep your mind clear. Spare your body. Let no manager persuade you that exhaustion is devotion to art, and no admirer that debauchery is freedom. They lied to me, but I invited the lie.”

He paused.

“And when the day comes—if it comes—when you feel the current weaken, when a phrase which once opened heaven becomes only a phrase, when the audience waits and you have nothing to give—go.”

She gazed at him.

“Leave the stage?”

“At once.”

“But if one still hopes?”

“Hope is then the cruellest prompter. It whispers lines belonging to yesterday.”

He leaned closer, speaking with sudden intensity.

“Go before they teach you. Do not wait for polite applause. Do not travel from town to town selling the memory of your face. Do not hate the young because they possess what has left you. Bow while they are still asking you to return. Then close the door yourself.”

The girl shivered.

“I cannot imagine it.”

“Of course not. Spring cannot imagine snow. But remember.”

Footsteps approached. Babanov emerged from the darkness carrying a ledger, his waistcoat unbuttoned and his face purple with indignation.

“Alexander Petrovitch! At last! I have searched everywhere. A fine business! We must discuss the repayment. The governor’s secretary threatens—”

He noticed Yureva and checked himself.

Kostromsky stood.

“How much do you owe me?”

“Your honorarium? After this catastrophe? Well, by the contract—though, strictly speaking, failure to complete—still, out of respect—”

“Keep it.”

Babanov blinked.

“Keep what?”

“All of it.”

“Seven hundred and fifty roubles?”

“Yes.”

The manager’s expression passed rapidly through suspicion, relief, and renewed alarm.

“But to-morrow—The Robbers. We must announce whether—”

“There will be no performance.”

“You need rest. By noon—”

“I shall be gone by noon.”

“But the tickets are sold!”

“Return the money.”

“With what?”

“With my seven hundred and fifty roubles. For the balance sell Hamlet’s crown.”

Babanov stared at him as one might stare at a madman whose madness has become inconveniently lucid.

“You cannot end your engagement in this fashion.”

“I have ended more than the engagement.”

“What shall I print?”

“Print the truth.”

“The truth? On a theatrical bill?”

Kostromsky almost laughed.

“Then print sudden illness. That is near enough.”

Babanov began another protest, but Kostromsky passed him. Yureva rose.

“Alexander Petrovitch!”

He turned.

She wished to say something worthy of the moment—something about gratitude, forgiveness, his greatness, her sorrow—but words failed her. She took his hand and kissed it.

He looked down at her bent head.

Once such homage would have seemed his right. Now it humbled him.

“Do not kiss that hand,” he said softly. “It struck at you.”

“It also showed me Hamlet.”

He withdrew his hand and touched her hair in blessing.

“Good-bye, Ophelia.”

Then he walked toward the stage.

No one stopped him. Babanov had begun calculating under his breath; Yureva remained beside the trunk; from a distant room came the laughter of two chorus girls already speaking of supper.

Kostromsky crossed between the heaps of discarded scenery. Denmark had vanished. The painted battlements leaned face downward; the arras lay rolled beside a broken throne; the graveyard spade rested upon a chair. Stagehands moved like indifferent executioners among the remains.

He paused at the line of the extinguished footlights.

The auditorium was empty.

How small it appeared without people! Nine hundred red seats, a tarnished chandelier, gilded boxes, the dark mouth of the gallery. Yet from that ordinary space had arisen the force which governed his life. He had feared it, seduced it, despised it, depended upon it. To-night it had judged him, not cruelly, not even consciously. The public had merely turned toward life where it found life.

There lay its innocence and its mercilessness.

Kostromsky bowed.

No applause answered.

He remained bent for an instant, then straightened and descended by the side passage. At the outer door the porter, half asleep, hurried to fetch his coat. Kostromsky put it on without assistance. The sable collar no longer seemed magnificent; under the weak lamp it showed its bald patches plainly.

Outside, snow had begun to fall.

The square before the theatre was deserted except for a few sledges moving toward the distant avenue. Posters bearing his enormous name fluttered on the walls. One had torn loose at the corner and snapped in the wind. Beneath KOSTROMSKY, in letters so small that they were scarcely visible, stood the name YUREVA.

He read it and smiled.

The cold air entered his lungs painfully, but it cleared his head. He did not know where he would go. The hotel, the railway station, another town—these had ceased to matter. For the first time in forty years there was no next performance awaiting him, no manager, no call-boy, no mirror, no audience breathing behind a curtain.

The emptiness was terrible.

It was also honest.

Behind him the theatre doors opened, and a workman threw out a bucket of dirty water. For a moment voices and hammering escaped into the night; then the doors closed, and silence returned.

Kostromsky walked across the square. His steps were slow but steady. At the corner he looked back once at the dim façade, at the posters, at the high window behind which Yureva perhaps still sat beneath the wavering gaslight.

“I have finished,” he said.

Snow settled upon his hat and shoulders, erasing his footprints almost as soon as he made them.

“I have finished.”

Mara,

At midnight on the last day of autumn, the clock in the drowned tower will ring.

Your father

At half past ten, Mara left Bellweather.

She wore her father’s green coat, which had been returned months after his disappearance by a fisherman who found it tangled in reeds. In one pocket she carried the map; in the other, a small traveling clock.

At the harbor, boats knocked softly against the piers. Mara chose the shopkeeper’s skiff, a broad little vessel used to collect crates from merchant ships. She left money under a stone, untied the rope, and rowed east.

The moon was full. The sea shone like a sheet of moving glass.

As the town receded, the ordinary sounds of land vanished. No cart wheels. No dogs. No tavern songs. Only the dip of the oars and the soft complaint of the rowlocks.

Mara followed the map past the Needle Rocks, then south toward a line of white foam where two currents met. At eleven, the tide drew back.

The sea began to change.

First she saw stones beneath the water—square stones, too regular to be natural. Then walls appeared in the moonlit depths. Chimneys. Roofs. A statue lying on its side. Long streets descended into green darkness, where pale fish moved through broken windows.

The drowned town.

At its center stood the clock tower.

Its uppermost chamber had emerged above the low tide. Water streamed from four enormous clock faces. Only one hand remained, pointing straight up.

Mara rowed closer.

A staircase wound around the tower’s exterior, beginning several feet below the surface. She tied the skiff to a carved stone figure and stepped into the freezing water.

The tower door stood open.

Inside, the air smelled of salt, rust, and something sweetly rotten. Moonlight entered through gaps in the stone. Mara climbed.

At the first landing, she found a room filled with furniture swollen by water. A table had been set for dinner. Plates rested before empty chairs. In one bowl lay an apple, fresh and red.

At the second landing, she heard children whispering behind a closed door.

At the third, someone knocked from inside the wall.

Mara did not stop.

The clock chamber waited at the top.

It was larger than her entire shop. Gears towered above her, their teeth encrusted with barnacles. Chains hung from the ceiling. Pools of black seawater trembled across the floor, though the machinery appeared motionless.

At the center stood her father.

He looked exactly as he had on his final morning.

His hair was dark, his shoulders broad, his hands scarred from years of metalwork. He wore no coat. One hand rested on a brass lever.

“Mara,” he said.

She had imagined this moment in a hundred ways. She had planned accusations and embraces. She had promised herself that, if she ever found him, she would remain calm.

Instead, she said, “You missed my seventeenth birthday.”

Her father’s face folded with grief.

“I know.”

“And my eighteenth.”

“I know.”

“Eleven of them.”

“I know.”

She crossed the room and struck him in the chest.

He staggered back. He was solid. Real.

Then she embraced him so fiercely that the tool case fell from her hand.

For a little while, neither spoke.

At last, Mara pulled away. “Did you send the letters?”

“Yes.”

“How?”

“The clock sends pieces of things forward. Sometimes seconds. Sometimes words. I wrote them years ago, but I never knew when they would reach you.”

“Years ago?” She looked at his unchanged face.

“For me, it has been three days.”

Outside, water dripped steadily from the tower walls.

He explained that he had come to destroy the black clapper. But once he reached the drowned clock, he discovered the clapper was not an object. It was one of the clock’s weights, shaped by the mechanism each time the appointed hour approached. Removing it from Saint Orra’s had only delayed the ringing.

“So you stayed here?”

“I stopped the mechanism.”

“For eleven years?”

“For Bellweather. For me, time barely passes inside the tower.”

Mara examined the lever beneath his hand. It was pulled halfway down, held in place by a loop of chain wrapped around his wrist.

“Why is it going to ring tonight?”

“Because I can’t hold it any longer.”

As if hearing him, the gears groaned.

Far below, something enormous shifted in the sea.

Mara opened the tool case. “Then we break it.”

“I have tried.”

“We remove the bell.”

“It has no bell.”

“Every clock can be stopped.”

“This is not a clock.”

“You said it was.”

“I was wrong.” He looked toward the streaming clock face. “It is a door that uses hours as hinges.”

A deep vibration passed through the tower. Mara’s traveling clock stopped.

Midnight.

Across the chamber, one of the giant gears moved.

Her father cried out as the chain tightened around his wrist. Mara seized the lever with both hands. It was cold enough to burn.

“Listen to me,” he said. “When it rings, Bellweather will answer. The eastern bell has no clapper now, but the tower will make one from whatever it can take.”

“Then Brother Ansel will stop it.”

“It will use iron from the roof. Blood from his body. A memory, if necessary. The answer always finds a way.”

“What do we do?”

Her father looked at the main clock face.

“Turn back the hand.”

Mara followed his gaze upward. The remaining hand stood at twelve, fixed to a central axle high above the floor.

“You told me it remakes possibilities,” she said.

“It exchanges them. If we turn the hand back one hour, the clock must find an hour to replace.”

“Whose hour?”

“I don’t know.”

Another gear shifted. Somewhere below, a bell began to draw breath.

Mara ran to the wall and climbed the iron maintenance ladder. Barnacles cut her palms. The tower shook beneath her. At the axle, she opened the small toolkit attached to her belt.

The mechanism was ancient, but its principles were familiar: locking pins, a ratchet wheel, an escapement shaped like two curved wings.

A moth.

She understood then why the symbol had marked the letters. It was the maker’s seal.

“Mara!” her father shouted.

The chain around his wrist was pulling him toward the machinery.

She drove a screwdriver beneath the locking pin. It did not move. She struck it with a hammer. Once. Twice.

The pin broke.

The great hand slipped backward by one minute.

The tower screamed.

Not metal. Not stone. Thousands of human voices cried out together.

Water burst through the clock faces. Mara clung to the ladder as the chamber flooded to her knees, her waist, her chest. Below, her father vanished under black water.

She reached for the axle and turned it.

Five minutes.

Ten.

Images filled the clock faces.

Bellweather’s streets appeared, bright beneath the moon. Every door in town stood open. Figures walked out of houses that had burned down long ago. Sailors climbed dripping from dry wells. Children called to mothers who had forgotten giving birth to them.

In Saint Orra’s tower, Brother Ansel clung to the black bell. A jagged spike of iron was growing from its hollow center.

Twenty minutes.

The axle tore skin from Mara’s palms.

The clock showed her other possibilities.

Her father returning the morning after the storm.

Her mother living past Mara’s infancy.

A larger shop on Market Square.

A husband whose face she almost recognized.

A daughter with Mara’s gray eyes.

All of it waited behind the turning hand, close enough to touch.

“Choose,” whispered the tower.

She almost released the axle.

Then she saw the cost.

Behind each restored life stood an absence. For her father to return, another father failed to come home. For her mother to live, a stranger’s mother died. The clock gave nothing. It merely moved grief from one heart to another.

Thirty minutes.

Below, her father surfaced. The chain had pulled his arm between two gears.

“Go back!” he gasped.

“I can free you.”

“No. Turn it forward again and go home.”

“If I turn it forward, the bell rings.”

“Then let it!”

Mara looked through the clock face toward Bellweather.

Even across the water, she saw its roofs beneath the moon. Her town. Its crooked chimneys, narrow streets, and tiny windows full of ordinary lives. Mr. Vale and his frightened wife. The schoolmaster. The young sailor who still wound his dead brother’s chronometer every morning. Brother Ansel in the church tower.

Forty minutes.

The tower’s whisper grew tender.

“Take the hour,” it said. “Take the life you lost.”

Mara thought of eleven birthdays. Eleven winters above a shop full of voices that could only tick. Eleven years of wondering whether her father had chosen to leave.

Then she saw him below, still fighting the gears, and knew he had chosen every day to stay.

Fifty minutes.

The axle resisted. The final ten marks seemed farther apart than all the others.

Her father stopped struggling.

“Mara,” he said quietly.

She looked down.

“If you finish, the clock will take its hour.”

“I know.”

“It may take the last hour of the town.”

“Or mine.”

“Yes.”

“Are you afraid?”

He smiled then, the same uneven smile she remembered from childhood.

“Always. Courage would be meaningless otherwise.”

Fifty-five minutes.

In the vision of Saint Orra’s, the black clapper was nearly complete.

Fifty-eight.

The eastern bell began to swing.

Fifty-nine.

Mara pulled with everything left in her.

The hand reached eleven.

The drowned clock rang.

The sound was too vast to hear. It passed through her bones, through the sea, through the foundations of Bellweather. For an instant, every star disappeared.

Then the clock took its hour.

Mara felt it searching.

It moved through the town, brushing sleepers and waking children. It entered houses, cellars, and graves. It opened every clock and touched every turning gear. It found births, deaths, promises, mistakes. It found countless hours of joy and suffering.

And then it found the hour inside the tower—the hour her father had held stretched across eleven years.

The clock took it.

The chain around his wrist vanished.

The gears shattered.

The hand broke free, spinning out into the night.

“Mara!” her father shouted.

The tower collapsed.

Cold water closed over her.

She remembered stone falling like rain. She remembered her father’s hand gripping hers. She remembered a red apple drifting upward from the room below.

Then there was only darkness.

Mara woke on the harbor steps at dawn.

Brother Ansel knelt beside her, soaked and shivering. Behind him, half the town crowded the waterfront.

“Where is he?” Mara asked.

No one answered.

She tried to stand.

A fisherman pointed toward the sea.

There, beyond the harbor wall, someone was rowing slowly through the morning mist.

The little skiff approached with one passenger: an old man in a torn shirt, his white hair shining in the dawn.

Mara knew him before she saw his face.

The clock had taken the hour her father had stretched—but when it returned time to its proper shape, it returned all of it.

He had aged eleven years in a single stroke.

Mara waded into the water before the boat touched shore.

Her father stepped out unsteadily. For a moment they simply looked at one another, measuring what time had changed.

“You’re late,” she said.

“I know.”

This time, when she embraced him, the clocks of Bellweather began to strike.

They did not agree on the hour. Some chimed six, others seven. Mr. Vale’s carriage clock struck thirteen. The church bells rang without anyone pulling their ropes.

But the eastern bell remained silent.

In the months that followed, Bellweather repaired what the sea had damaged. A few doors continued to open into unfamiliar rooms. One alley led to the harbor on Tuesdays and to a wheat field on Fridays. Names appeared on old graves, though no one could identify them.

The townspeople learned to live with these things.

Mara’s father returned to the shop, but he no longer repaired clocks. He said he had spent enough of his life inside them. Instead, he made wooden boats and kept each one on a shelf, never putting them in water.

Mara sealed the map inside the oldest clock case. She also kept the three letters, though the ink faded until only the moths remained.

Years later, a child visiting the shop asked why none of the clocks showed the same time.

Mara considered giving the usual answer: different mechanisms, uneven springs, careless winding.

Instead, she lifted the child so she could hear the ticking inside a tall walnut clock.

“Every clock tells the truth,” Mara said. “But none of them tells the whole truth.”

The child frowned. “Then how do we know what time it is?”

“We don’t,” Mara replied. “We only know what we choose to do with it.”

Outside, Bellweather leaned into the wind. The sea glittered beyond the rooftops, keeping its drowned streets and broken tower beneath the waves.

On the shop wall, a small clock with a moth engraved on its face stopped for exactly one minute.

Mara noticed.

She waited.

Then the clock began to tick again.
